meta.theme: forgiveness made a duty becomes collectable and stops being forgiveness; forgiveness never owed leaves a fully repentant wrongdoer at the mercy of the wronged; the usual escapes each drop one horn

source.usage_note: Original composition in CAT register for CAT OS; no external source adapted.

meta.reviewer_notes: A genuine aporia in the first person, which the corpus has only twice, written slowly with sentences averaging well over twenty-four words. The two escapes are not straw: each is tested and found to keep one horn by dropping the other, which is the mechanism underneath the mood. The near-tie is in the assumption question, where a distractor moves the hinge from the other person's standing to reproach to the giver's own feeling. The detail question is on the first escape, so that the key cannot be read off the final paragraph. The move is an aporia that holds two commitments without resolving them, carried in a puzzled, slow, first-person-singular voice of long sentences.

quality.adversarial_review: Q1: A strong candidate argues for the reproach option, since reproach is the sharpest failure in the paragraph. The text assigns it to the second escape by the sentence "If it is bad of me to refuse, then he may reproach me", while the first escape's failure is in the words "making him irrelevant". Q2: The rival is the option fusing "stop pressing a claim" with "stop holding the wrong against him"; the text's "not merely ... but" separates them, and the key is settled by "worth wanting was that it could not be extracted". Q3: The gift-it-would-be-bad-not-to-give option is argued for because the author wants forgiveness to remain free; it is killed by "a debt under another name", which is the author's verdict on exactly that view. Q4: The giver's-feeling option is the near-tie; it is killed by the joint "then he may reproach me for refusing", which puts the hinge in the other person's standing, and the negation test: if standing to reproach did not mark a debt, the conclusion would not follow.

paragraphs.text: For weeks I have been trying to decide whether forgiveness can be owed, and whichever answer I settle on in the morning is intolerable by the evening. Suppose a man has wronged me and has then done everything that could be asked of him: admitted the wrong without excuse, repaired what could be repaired, and changed so that a repetition is unlikely. Surely I now owe him forgiveness. Yet the moment I say that I owe it, something odd happens to the thing I am supposed to owe. A debt can be demanded. If forgiveness is owed once repentance is complete, then he may stand before me and require it, and if I refuse he has a grievance against me: the wronged person has, by being repented to, become a defaulter.

That cannot be right, because what made forgiveness worth wanting was that it could not be extracted. What he wants from me is not merely that I stop pressing a claim, but that I stop holding the wrong against him, that I give up a resentment I was entitled to. A resentment surrendered on demand is not surrendered; it is confiscated. So forgiveness, if it is to remain forgiveness, must be something I am free not to give. But if it is never owed, then I hold, for as long as I like, a power over a person who has done everything that could be asked, and nothing he does can reach it. It looks less like a moral prerogative than a licence for cruelty.

I have tried the usual escapes. One says that forgiveness is owed, but to oneself: a resentment kept past its usefulness corrodes the person who keeps it, and so I ought to let it go for my own sake. This saves the freedom, because he cannot demand what I owe myself, but it saves it by making him irrelevant, which is strange, since it was his repentance that was supposed to change what I ought to do. A second escape says that forgiveness is a gift, but a gift it would be bad of me not to give, as it would be bad to walk past a drowning child I was under no contract to save. This keeps his claim on me, but the word "bad" is now doing the work the word "owed" was forbidden to do. If it is bad of me to refuse, then he may reproach me for refusing, and a gift that may be reproached when it is not given is a debt under another name.

So each escape keeps one of my commitments by quietly dropping the other, and I suspect they cannot both be kept. Either forgiveness answers to what he has done, in which case his doing enough gives him standing to require it, or it answers only to me, in which case his doing enough gives him nothing at all. I do not know which I would sooner give up. What I do know is that whenever someone tells me that forgiveness is a duty, I want to ask what they think will be left of it once it has been collected; and whenever someone tells me that it is always a free gift, I want to ask what should be said to the man still standing there, having done everything.

questions.target_mistake: confusing the failure of the first escape (the wrongdoer drops out) with the failure of the second (reproach turns the gift into a debt)
questions.stem: According to the passage, the escape that makes forgiveness owed to oneself fails because it

options.A: makes the wrongdoer's repentance irrelevant to what the wronged person ought to do.
options.B: applies only where the wrongdoer has not yet repaired what he was able to repair.
options.C: treats the wronged person's own good as a reason that cannot alter what she ought to do.
options.D: permits the wrongdoer to reproach the wronged person for withholding what is a gift.

explanation.expert_notice: The third paragraph tests two escapes in turn and gives each its own failure. The first, forgiveness "owed, but to oneself", is faulted in one clause: "it saves it by making him irrelevant, which is strange, since it was his repentance that was supposed to change what I ought to do". The expert locates that clause before looking at the options.
explanation.correct_reasoning: The text says the first escape "saves the freedom, because he cannot demand what I owe myself, but it saves it by making him irrelevant". Irrelevant to what? To "what I ought to do", which "his repentance ... was supposed to change". The correct option restates exactly that: the wrongdoer's repentance no longer bears on the wronged person's duty.
explanation.question_type_note: A detail question on a passage with two parallel cases is really a matching question: which fault goes with which case. Find the sentence, not the paragraph.
explanation.reading_habit: When a paragraph says "One says ... A second ...", draw a line between the two before answering anything about either; most wrong options here are the right fact attached to the wrong case.

distractors.why_wrong: The first escape is about the resentment's usefulness to the person who keeps it; nothing ties it to whether repair has been done, and the whole passage assumes a man who has "repaired what could be repaired".
distractors.seductive_element: The phrase "past its usefulness" invites a reader to supply a condition about when it stops being useful, and repair is the obvious candidate.

distractors.why_wrong: The escape says the opposite: "I ought to let it go for my own sake", so one's own good is precisely what alters what one ought to do. The option keeps the vocabulary of "own good" and reverses its role.
distractors.seductive_element: It uses the passage's own words about the self and reads like a criticism, which is what the question asks for.

distractors.why_wrong: Reproach belongs to the second escape: "If it is bad of me to refuse, then he may reproach me for refusing". The first escape blocks demand altogether, since "he cannot demand what I owe myself".
distractors.seductive_element: It is a real failure named in the same paragraph, and the two escapes are only a sentence apart.

questions.target_mistake: accepting an option that is merely compatible with the paragraph instead of one that follows from it
questions.prediction_target: since what made forgiveness worth wanting is that it cannot be extracted, any forgiveness that could be compelled would not be what the wrongdoer wanted
questions.stem: If the author's reasoning in the second paragraph is sound, which of the following must be true?

options.A: Resentment that is given up freely is always given up for the wrongdoer's sake.
options.B: The wronged person was never entitled to the resentment she is asked to surrender.
options.C: A forgiveness that the wrongdoer could compel would not be the thing he wanted.
options.D: Ceasing to press a claim and ceasing to hold a wrong against someone are the same act.

explanation.expert_notice: The second paragraph has two linked claims: forgiveness was "worth wanting" because "it could not be extracted", and what the wrongdoer wants is that the wronged person "give up a resentment I was entitled to", which "surrendered on demand is not surrendered; it is confiscated". Put together, those say that a compelled forgiveness is not the thing wanted.
explanation.correct_reasoning: If what he wants is a surrender that cannot be extracted, then a forgiveness he could compel is by definition extracted, and the text says of such a surrender that it "is confiscated", not given. So he would not have got what he wanted. That follows from the paragraph without any added premise, which is what "must be true" requires.
explanation.question_type_note: A must-be-true option is one the passage cannot be true without. Test each option by asking: could the paragraph stand exactly as written and this option still be false? If yes, it is not forced.
explanation.reading_habit: For must-be-true questions, prefer the option that merely combines two sentences already in the text over any option that adds a word like "always", "never" or "the same".

distractors.why_wrong: The paragraph says nothing about why a free surrender is made; it says only that it must be free. "always ... for the wrongdoer's sake" is a new and absolute claim that the text neither states nor needs.
distractors.seductive_element: It sounds like the generous reading of forgiveness, and generosity is in the air of the passage.

distractors.why_wrong: The author says the wronged person gives up "a resentment I was entitled to". Entitlement is affirmed, not denied; the option reverses it.
distractors.seductive_element: The author is uneasy about keeping the resentment, and a reader may slide from being uneasy about keeping it to not being entitled to it.

distractors.why_wrong: The text separates the two: what he wants is "not merely that I stop pressing a claim, but that I stop holding the wrong against him". The option fuses what the author took care to split.
distractors.seductive_element: Both phrases come from one sentence, so they look like two ways of saying one thing.

questions.target_mistake: taking one of the "usual escapes" the author tries and rejects as the author's own view
questions.prediction_target: the author holds both commitments and rejects both escapes, so he would agree only with a statement that presses a question on one side rather than one that resolves the dilemma
questions.stem: With which of the following would the author most likely agree?

options.A: Whether forgiveness is owed can be settled by first deciding whether the repentance was sincere enough.
options.B: Anyone who calls forgiveness a duty should say what will be left of it once it has been collected.
options.C: Forgiveness is best understood as a gift that it would be bad of the wronged person not to give.
options.D: A person who keeps a resentment beyond its usefulness thereby wrongs the person he resents.

explanation.expert_notice: The passage is an aporia: it ends "I do not know which I would sooner give up". So any option that resolves the question is suspect. What the author does commit to is the challenge in the final paragraph: to the duty view, "what they think will be left of it once it has been collected".
explanation.correct_reasoning: The last paragraph states, in the author's own voice, that when someone calls forgiveness a duty, "I want to ask what they think will be left of it once it has been collected". The correct option turns that wish into a demand on the duty view, which is exactly the author's position: the duty view owes an account of what collection leaves behind. He does not say the duty view is false, only that it must answer this.
explanation.question_type_note: An agree-disagree question on an aporia almost never has a key that settles the matter. Look for the option that states a burden the author places on one side, and reject options that pick a side for him.
explanation.reading_habit: Separate the views an author tries on ("I have tried the usual escapes") from the views he holds. A view introduced in order to be tested is not the author's, however sympathetically it is stated.

distractors.why_wrong: The dilemma is set up for a man who has "done everything that could be asked", so sincerity is assumed from the start and the problem remains. Settling sincerity does not settle the question.
distractors.seductive_element: Sincere repentance is in the passage's first paragraph, and a reader may take the stage-setting for the solution.

distractors.why_wrong: This is the second escape, and the author rejects it: "a gift that may be reproached when it is not given is a debt under another name".
distractors.seductive_element: It is stated sympathetically and at length, and "gift" is the word the author uses for what forgiveness should remain.

distractors.why_wrong: The first escape says that a resentment kept too long "corrodes the person who keeps it", a harm to the keeper; it never says it wrongs the person resented, and the author rejects the escape anyway.
distractors.seductive_element: It feels like the moral of the first escape, and "wrongs" sounds like a stronger version of "corrodes".

questions.target_mistake: locating the hinge of the argument in the giver's feeling rather than in the other person's standing to reproach
questions.prediction_target: the step from "he may reproach me for refusing" to "a debt under another name" needs the premise that being open to reproach for refusing is what distinguishes a debt from a gift
questions.stem: The author's conclusion that "a gift that may be reproached when it is not given is a debt under another name" depends on which of the following assumptions?

options.A: What makes something a gift rather than a debt is whether the giver would feel bad about refusing it.
options.B: A person who walks past a drowning child has, in doing so, incurred a debt to the child.
options.C: The wronged person is more likely to forgive when reproach is permitted than when it is not.
options.D: What marks a debt off from a gift is whether the other person has standing to reproach a refusal.

explanation.expert_notice: Trace the chain: "If it is bad of me to refuse, then he may reproach me for refusing, and a gift that may be reproached when it is not given is a debt". The conclusion is reached through "he may reproach me", so the unstated premise must connect reproach to debt. Whatever the expert writes down before looking should contain the word "reproach".
explanation.correct_reasoning: The argument moves from "bad of me to refuse" to "he may reproach me" to "a debt under another name". The only bridge that makes the last step valid is that the other person's standing to reproach a refusal is what distinguishes a debt from a gift. Deny that premise, and a gift could be reproachable and still a gift, so the conclusion would not follow. That is the test of an assumption: remove it and the argument falls.
explanation.question_type_note: An assumption question asks for the premise the author uses without stating. Find the exact words through which the conclusion is reached and ask what has to be true for that step to work. Then negate your candidate: if the argument survives the negation, it was not the assumption.
explanation.reading_habit: In a chain of "if ... then ... and", the assumption lives at the joint between the last two links. Quote the joint before you read the options.

distractors.why_wrong: The chain passes through "he may reproach me", the other person's standing, not through how the giver feels. If the hinge were the giver's own feeling, the step "then he may reproach me" would be doing nothing.
distractors.seductive_element: It has the right form (what distinguishes a gift from a debt) and the passage does say "bad of me", so a reader can mistake the giver's badness for the hinge.

distractors.why_wrong: The drowning child is an illustration of what "bad of me not to give" means; the argument's conclusion does not depend on classifying that case as a debt, and the author never says it is one.
distractors.seductive_element: The example is vivid and sits in the same sentence as the premise it illustrates.

distractors.why_wrong: Whether reproach makes forgiveness more likely is an empirical question the passage never raises; the conclusion is about what forgiveness is, not about when it occurs.
distractors.seductive_element: It mentions reproach, which is the right joint, and sounds like a plausible thing to assume.

vocabulary.passage_use: that it could not be extracted
vocabulary.meaning_here: drawn out of someone by pressure or force rather than freely given

vocabulary.passage_use: less like a moral prerogative than a licence for cruelty
vocabulary.meaning_here: a right or privilege that belongs to a particular person

vocabulary.passage_use: he may reproach me for refusing
vocabulary.meaning_here: to blame someone to their face for having done wrong

mentor.challenge: He has admitted it, repaired it, changed. Everything that could be asked of him is done. Do you now owe him forgiveness? And if you do, what is left of it?
mentor.one_sentence_summary: A first-person essay works through a genuine puzzle, that forgiveness cannot be owed as a duty without becoming a demandable debt that stops being forgiveness, yet if it is never owed the wronged person holds an answerable power over someone who has done everything that could be asked, and neither of the usual escapes resolves it.
mentor.main_idea: The writer cannot decide whether forgiveness can be owed: making it a duty lets the wrongdoer demand it, which confiscates rather than grants it, but refusing to owe it at all leaves a fully repentant wrongdoer permanently at the wronged person's mercy. Two common escapes each save one side of the problem only by giving up the other.
mentor.simple_explanation:
The writer has spent weeks trying to decide whether forgiveness can be owed, and cannot settle it. Imagine someone wronged you and then did everything right: admitted it plainly, fixed what could be fixed, and changed so it will not happen again. It feels like you now owe him forgiveness. But the moment forgiveness becomes something owed, it turns into a debt, and a debt can be demanded. If he can demand it and you refuse, you are now the one in the wrong, which feels backwards.

That cannot be right either, because what made forgiveness worth having was exactly that it could not be forced out of you. What the wrongdoer really wants is not just that you drop your complaint, but that you genuinely stop holding the wrong against him, and a resentment you were forced to give up is not given, it is taken. So forgiveness has to stay something you are free to withhold. But if it is never owed, you can hold onto it forever no matter what he does, which starts to look less like a right and more like a licence to be cruel.

The writer tries two ways out. The first says you owe forgiveness to yourself, because holding a grudge too long harms you, not him. This keeps your freedom, since you cannot be made to pay a debt you owe only yourself, but it does so by making the wrongdoer's repentance pointless, which is strange, because his changing was supposed to be what mattered. The second way says forgiveness is a gift, just one it would be unkind not to give, the way it would be unkind to walk past a drowning child. This keeps his claim on you alive, but now if it is unkind to refuse, he can reproach you for refusing, and a gift you can be blamed for withholding is really just a debt by another name.

So each escape only works by quietly giving up half of what the writer wants to be true. Either forgiveness depends on what the wrongdoer did, in which case doing enough gives him the right to demand it, or it depends only on you, in which case nothing he does earns him anything. The writer does not know which half to give up. All he knows is that anyone who calls forgiveness a duty should explain what is left of it once it can be collected, and anyone who calls it a pure free gift should explain what to say to the man still standing there, having done everything that could possibly be asked.
mentor.why_difficult: The passage never resolves into a clean answer, and both of the 'escapes' it tries are stated sympathetically enough that a reader can mistake either one for the writer's actual view; the fourth paragraph's refusal to choose is the point, not a loose end, and the questions test whether a reader can tell the difference between a position the writer tries on and a burden he places on both sides of the question.
mentor.author_intention: To lay out, honestly and without faking a resolution, why forgiveness resists being treated as either a duty or a pure gift, and to leave the reader holding the same unresolved question the writer holds.

paragraph_journey.note: If forgiveness is owed once someone has fully repented, it becomes a debt he can demand, which feels wrong.
But if forgiveness can never be demanded, the wronged person can withhold it forever, which looks like a licence for cruelty.
Owing it only to yourself drops the wrongdoer from the picture; calling it a gift that would be unkind to refuse lets him reproach you, making it a debt again.
Each escape only works by giving up half of what the writer wants, and he ends by challenging both the duty view and the free-gift view rather than choosing one.

mentor.tone_progression: The voice is puzzled and candid from the first sentence, admitting the problem cannot be settled; it stays searching and slow through the two middle paragraphs as it tests each escape, and ends not in resolution but in two pointed questions aimed at whichever side the reader is tempted to take.
key_transitions: 'That cannot be right, because what made forgiveness worth wanting was that it could not be extracted.' (opening of the second paragraph): the dilemma flips from forgiveness as owed to forgiveness as necessarily free.
'I have tried the usual escapes.' (opening of the third paragraph): the essay turns from stating the problem to testing the standard ways out of it.
mentor.misunderstanding: A reader who likes tidy endings assumes the passage must come down on one side, and reads whichever escape is stated most sympathetically, usually the gift view, as the writer's real position; the fourth paragraph says plainly that the writer does not know which commitment he would give up, so neither escape is endorsed.
mentor.traps_summary: The wrong options give the fault of one escape to the other, state as settled something the writer leaves open, or hand the writer a resolved position when his stated end point is two unanswered questions aimed at both sides.
mentor.reading_lesson: When a writer says 'I have tried the usual escapes' before describing a view, that view is being tested, not held; keep a clear line between a position an author introduces to examine and a position the author actually occupies, however sympathetically the tested view is written.
mentor.real_world: The same tension appears in any situation where someone who has done everything right still depends on another person's unforced goodwill, from an apology to a reference, a reconciliation, or a second chance at trust.
mentor.takeaway: A forgiveness that can be demanded has already stopped being forgiveness, but a forgiveness that is never owed can become a permanent power over someone who has done everything that could be asked.
mentor.reflection_question: If someone wronged you and did everything that could be asked to make it right, would you say you still owe them nothing, or would that feel like its own kind of unfairness?

eli10.big_idea: Forgiving someone cannot be a rule you must follow, because then it could be demanded, but if it is never owed at all, a person who has done everything right still has no claim on you.
eli10.story: Imagine someone hurt you. Later, he says sorry, fixes what he broke, and changes so it will not happen again. He has done everything right. So do you now have to forgive him? The writer says maybe not. If forgiveness must be given, then he can demand it. And a demanded gift is not really a gift at all. But if forgiveness never has to be given, you could refuse forever, even though he did everything right. That feels unfair too. The writer tries two fixes. One says forgive for your own peace of mind. But then the other person stops mattering at all. The other says forgiveness is a kind gift. But then refusing it makes you look bad, which means people can push you after all. Neither fix works cleanly. The writer admits he does not know the answer.
paragraphs: The writer wonders if forgiving someone becomes something they can demand once they have truly made things right.
He decides forgiveness cannot be forced, but then a fully sorry person might never get it, which seems unfair too.
He tries two fixes: forgiving for your own sake, or calling it a kind gift, and both break down.
He ends without an answer, asking hard questions of anyone sure that forgiveness is either a duty or a free gift.
eli10.author_view: The writer is honestly stuck, not pretending to have an answer, and wants the reader to feel the same pull between two ideas that cannot both be fully true.
